sources.headline: They Fled Ethiopia’s War. Now, Israel May Send Them Back.
sources.text:
JERUSALEM—For 75 days starting in 2020, Luwam Habteab slept on the floor of a prison cell, given little food and no medical care. She was detained that November by Ethiopian security forces for her reporting on the Axum massacre, in which Eritrean forces killed hundreds of civilians over a weekend—one of the deadliest episodes of the 2020-22 Tigray war.
Upon her release, Habteab found that her apartment had been sealed by federal police. Her family had warned her not to return there, telling her that security forces were waiting. A local archbishop with a connection at the Israeli Embassy interceded, after which Habteab was ushered out of the country. She landed in Tel Aviv in August 2023 and applied for asylum. (Habteab is identified by a pseudonym out of fear of reprisal.)
Habteab now lives in Jerusalem’s Old City, where she spends most of her days praying. As of August, she was one of 1,334 Ethiopians with open asylum claims before Israel’s Interior Ministry, according to figures that the ministry confirmed to Foreign Policy.
Months after Habteab arrived, in January 2024, the Israeli Interior Ministry determined that the situation in Ethiopia was stable enough to send its nationals home, revoking the group protection that had shielded asylum-seekers from deportation. That stability did not last: This July, Tigray’s regional authorities declared that the 2022 peace agreement with the federal government had collapsed, accusing Addis Ababa of preparing for war.
A multistory residential building featuring open walkways with railings surrounding a central courtyard. In the foreground, laundry hangs from a clothesline, and a profile of a person in a scarf is visible on the right as she passes by the clothes.
A woman walks past clothes left to dry on the balcony of a school used as shelter at a camp for displaced people in Mekelle, in Ethiopia’s Tigray region, on July 19, 2024. Michele Spatari/AFP via Getty Images
Last month, an alliance of rebel groups launched a full-scale offensive against federal forces, seizing airports across Tigray and pushing into neighboring Afar and Amhara states. Federal forces have since retaken Tigray’s capital, though the rebels have vowed to keep fighting; Eritrea and Ethiopia have cut diplomatic ties. Explosions have been reported in Addis Ababa, which Israeli authorities say is safe for returnees.
Habteab has watched with dread as the fighting returned to her home province. Much of Tigray is under a communications blackout, reviving fears of the total siege during the 2020-22 war that starved the region and killed as many as 600,000 people. Habteab’s family in Tigray is almost impossible to reach, she said.
With Israel’s national elections set for Oct. 27, civil society advocates warn that right-wing politicians are once again casting asylum-seekers as a threat to gain a leg up. Israeli officials refer to some migrants and refugees as “infiltrators,” a term embedded in the country’s own laws, and successive governments have described their presence as a danger to Israel’s Jewish character.
Habteab and other asylum-seekers in Israel have few places left to go as domestic politics turn against them and Western governments dismantle the asylum system that was supposed to protect them.
A group of people wearing white garments gather inside a dimly lit stone room. Many hold lit candles, and several individuals hold prayer books or smartphones. Almost everyone has their head covered with either a scarf or a hat.
Ethiopian Orthodox Christian pilgrims light candles during a ceremony on the roof of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem’s Old City on April 19, 2025. John Wessels/AFP via Getty Images
Israel has a long history with the notion of asylum. Founded by refugees in the wake of the Holocaust as a safe haven for the Jewish diaspora, the country was among the first signatories of the 1951 Refugee Convention. Jewish jurists were instrumental in shaping the convention’s core nonrefoulement principle, the rule that no one may be returned to a country where their life is at risk.
Yet, since the Israeli government took over processing asylum claims from the United Nations in 2009, it has granted asylum status to less than 1 percent of those seeking it, according to HIAS Israel, a Jewish humanitarian nonprofit.
Israel has also long held a place in the imagination of Ethiopian asylum-seekers as the land of the ancient Israelites, in whose story of exile and return they saw themselves. In practical terms, the country was also the closest state offering asylum that they could reach without undertaking the perilous Mediterranean crossing.
Of the Ethiopians in Israel who are not Jewish, some—such as Habteab—fled during the Tigray war and its aftermath. But most have been in Israel for a decade or more, arriving on pilgrimage visas or by crossing the Egyptian border before Israel completed its fence there in 2013. They, too, are asylum-seekers: Almost all applied for protection after arriving, having fled earlier rounds of interethnic violence and state persecution, according to the Jerusalem African Community Center (JACC), a support and advocacy organization for the city’s African asylum-seekers.
On arrival, they opened asylum claims with the Interior Ministry and were interviewed about why they had come to Israel. Under Israeli law, the ministry was meant to review each claim and decide whether to grant refugee status—a process that, for most of these asylum-seekers, didn’t happen. Now, according to advocates, many Ethiopian applicants are being summoned back after more than a decade for a second interview to determine whether they can stay in Israel.
An overhead view shows a large crowd of hundreds of people gathered outdoors in an open space. Several national flags are raised above the crowd, including the flags of Israel, Ethiopia, and Eritrea, while speakers stand on a platform with microphones.
Demonstrators wave the former Ethiopian flag, the Eritrean flag, and the Israeli flag as thousands of African asylum-seekers protest against the detention of immigrants and widespread refusal to grant refugee status, seen in Tel Aviv, Israel, on Jan. 5, 2014.Jack Guez/AFP via Getty Images
Asked for comment, Israel’s Population and Immigration Authority said, “there is no policy of deportation regarding this group” and that cases are examined individually. The authority added that it does not determine whether a country is safe for returnees, referring questions to the Israeli Foreign Ministry. (The Foreign Ministry did not respond to a request for comment.)
Anat Ben-Dor, who runs the Refugee Rights Clinic at Tel Aviv University, said the burden of proof placed on applicants for asylum to establish a credible fear of persecution is set very high and that interviewers look for inconsistencies between what an applicant says now and what they said on arrival.
“The whole interview is actually an effort not to find the truth, but to find flaws and problems in the testimony,” Ben-Dor said. “Very few people can successfully pass such an interview, particularly when the system is so slow that people are being interviewed about events that sometimes occurred 10 years earlier.”
Asked whether the system was dysfunctional or intentionally obstructive, Michal Pomeranz, another lawyer who represents asylum-seekers, said it was both. “They clearly want to make people’s lives here miserable, and that’s something even the Supreme Court has said,” she said, referring to a 2020 ruling that struck down a law requiring asylum-seekers to deposit 20 percent of their wages into a fund that they could recover only by leaving the country.
After the follow-up interview, the Interior Ministry decides whether an asylum-seeker may stay in Israel or must leave—but the outcome is almost always the same, according to Yael Paul Strauss, who runs the psychosocial department at JACC.
By her account, 90 percent to 95 percent of those summoned are rejected and given three to four months to leave the country. “It’s presented as giving them another chance, but in reality, they’re just being called in to be told they have to leave,” Paul Strauss said.
The cost of contesting a rejection is steep, running at around $4,000 to petition a denied application and another $4,000 for an appeal, according to Paul Strauss. Few employers will hire someone with a temporary permit, regardless of their profession or level of education in Ethiopia, leaving most asylum-seekers with few ways to raise that kind of money.
Paul Strauss described a message that she had recently received from a mother of three small children who had paid to appeal her asylum rejection, lost, and had no idea where she would find the money to try again. “She turns to me, ‘Please help me, save my life,’ and I have nothing to give her,” Paul Strauss said.
Two people wearing blue medical scrubs walk away from the camera up steps toward the entrance of a brick building. A blue and white sign planted on the lawn in the foreground reads "VOTE HERE".
A former refugee from Ethiopia (left) arrives to vote for the first time at a polling station in Clarkston, Georgia, in the United States on Nov. 5, 2024. Yasuyoshi Chiba/AFP via Getty Images
For many Ethiopian asylum-seekers, the answer to Israel’s stonewalling was to seek resettlement in a third country, another cornerstone of asylum law. For years, the main destination was the United States, which accepted a small number of the most vulnerable cases referred by the U.N. However, that route is now all but closed.
When he returned to office in 2025, U.S. President Donald Trump effectively dismantled the U.S. refugee admissions program and suspended the entry of all refugees into the country, including those who had already been screened. Following legal challenges, the Trump administration resumed limited admissions under a historically low cap of 7,500 refugees for fiscal year 2026—admissions that have been allocated almost entirely to white South African Afrikaners.
In December 2025, the Trump administration also terminated the temporary protected status that Ethiopians were granted during the Tigray war. Around 900 asylum-seekers in Israel—mainly Sudanese and Eritrean, along with some Ethiopians—were in the pipeline to be resettled to the United States as of early 2025, according to Sivan Carmel, the country director of HIAS Israel, which processed the cases.
Some had already cleared their medical and security checks, had departure dates, and needed only plane tickets. “They’d left their jobs; they’d already told their landlords they’d be leaving” before their entry to the United States was denied, Carmel said.
The office of the U.N. refugee agency in Israel, which referred those cases and managed resettlement out of the country, has been hollowed out as part of the same pattern of global retrenchment against asylum—its staff reduced to three and its Tel Aviv office cut. Agency staff struggle to keep up with the thousands of open asylum claims.
This has left the work to fall to groups such as JACC, which operates on a shoestring budget. Paul Strauss spends hours filling in resettlement forms with families who cannot afford a lawyer. Each time Paul Strauss submits a file, she said, the U.N. representative reminds her that completing it does not guarantee placement elsewhere.
For those who cannot leave for another country and cannot stay in Israel, the return of war to Ethiopia has taken away their last consolation: the hope that the danger that they fled might be in the past. As armed forces push toward Ethiopia’s capital and much of Tigray remains in the dark, many of the families that Israel intends to send back can’t even get in touch with their relatives.
For those working on behalf of the asylum-seekers, the bigger picture is not lost. “I want to live in a state that I’m not embarrassed by,” Pomeranz said. “I kept thinking things couldn’t get worse. They keep getting worse.”

sources.headline: Fighting in Ethiopia and the Risk of Regional Spillover
sources.text:
In September, fighting broke out in Ethiopia’s Tigray region between Ethiopian government forces and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), effectively collapsing the 2022 peace deal. In October, Ethiopian forces recaptured an airport and towns from the TPLF and started moving closer to the border with Eritrea. The renewed conflict raised concerns about both increased instability within Ethiopia — particularly as the TPLF joined with several other armed groups under a new Alliance for Survival — and the potential for a new war between Ethiopia and Eritrea. Ethiopia accused Eritrea of supporting the TPLF and sending its own forces across the border into Tigray. The two countries severed diplomatic ties.Increased conflict in northern Ethiopia comes amid longstanding regional tensions, including disputes over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam’s impact on the Nile River and landlocked Ethiopia’s ambitions to gain direct access to the sea. We asked five experts to assess the risks that the conflict in Tigray poses for Ethiopia, Eritrea, Somalia, Sudan, and Egypt.Read more below.William Davison Editor with Africa Confidential Founder of Ethiopia Insight Although unlikely, the biggest risk for Ethiopia is state collapse. This could occur if the TPLF produces stiff resistance that in turn boosts insurgencies in Amhara and Oromia, leading to a rebel march on Addis Ababa — a recipe for worsening disorder.A less dramatic risk is that the federal military gets bogged down in Tigray as the TPLF mounts an insurgency with support from Eritrea. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government would then lose ground against rebels elsewhere. While not an existential threat, this scenario would deepen Ethiopia’s insecurity.The most achievable upside is defeat of the TPLF, the driving force of ethnonationalism. This would mean the failure of the rebel coalition, allowing Abiy to push ahead with constitutional reforms that centralize power and de-ethnicize the federation.If

sources.headline: French students are showing us what protest looks like in the age of viral spectacle
sources.text:
The recent wave of protests in Europe have left us with two striking, viral spectacles of violence and joy. As Limoges’ historic town hall went up in flames, the Orchestre du Nouveau Monde was playing classical music in Paris’ central Place de la République (until the musicians were teargassed by police, that is).
Fire at Limoges Town Hall (Haute-Vienne, France), October 17, 2026.
Lucas Destrem/Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA
Both scenes offer radically different ways of seeing the protests. The burning town hall offers a powerful image of destruction; the orchestra, of anti-authoritarian collective solidarity. Neither tells the whole story, but their contrast raises important questions: which image will come to represent the protests, and who decides what we see?
France’s demonstrations began with students protesting deteriorating school conditions, including staff shortages and dilapidated buildings. But they quickly intersected with broader anger over living costs and public services.
The unrest also formed part of a wider European moment. On the same weekend, people took to the streets in Spain, Italy, Belgium, Portugal and Albania. Grievances include low wages, rising energy prices and unaffordable housing, each within its own national context.
These were separate mobilisations, not a single coordinated movement. Yet they reveal how different struggles are being represented in an age where everything – including a mass protest movement – can go viral.
A rally or a riot?
The battle over meaning starts with language.
On October 19, the European Commission condemned looting as “unacceptable” while stressing that peaceful protest must be protected.
In the European Parliament, the centre-right European People’s Party, backed by the European Conservatives and Reformists, has framed the unrest as an ideological threat, proposing a debate titled “France, Italy and Belgium: Latest anti-democratic violence by radical far-left groups”.
These interventions reflect a broader contest over whether demonstrations should be understood primarily as expressions of social grievances, or as challenges to public order. Political leaders across Europe have sought to steer this debate.
In France and Italy, Emmanuel Macron and Giorgia Meloni distinguished between people’s right to demonstrate and violent delinquents.
However, other politicians such as French far-right leader Marine Le Pen have blamed the far left and immigrants. In Spain, Madrid’s regional leader Isabel Díaz Ayuso pointed to the “anti-democratic left”, while Albania’s socialist Prime Minister Edi Rama described the protesters as being radicalised by “antifa”.
On October 17, demonstrators gathered around Place de la République amid tear gas. Cars and rental bikes were set on fire on Boulevard Voltaire.
Jorge Jaramillo/Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA
The name we give to these gatherings – rally, riot, protest – matters greatly, as it shapes public and policy perceptions of what is legitimate in democratic societies. This, in turn, decides what kind of response – in particular what level of violence and repression – people will accept in addressing them.
Disruptive protests are typically presented negatively in both political discourse and in the mainstream media, regardless of an outlet’s political stance. This happens by connecting protest to violence, ideological extremism and threats to democratic legitimacy, thus discrediting protesters and their demands.
This means isolated violence can come to represent an entire demonstration or movement. On October 17, over half a million protesters took to the streets across France, but these historic, peaceful demonstrations have been completely eclipsed by media coverage of the looting that ensued.
Read more:
France’s ‘casseurs’: why the term fails to do justice to the extent of looting and spiralling unrest
Gen Z protest symbols
At Place de la République, the Orchestre du Nouveau Monde brought together hundreds of musicians to play popular, well-known pieces like the anti-fascist anthem Bella Ciao, along with songs from The Avengers and The Hunger Games.
The concert did not, of course, make the conflict disappear. What it offered was another way to see it, not simply as a confrontation between police and disorderly crowds, but as a collective performance of resistance.
Gen Z’s cultural symbols have also played a key role in generating viral spectacles. In France, students have appeared dressed as Batman, Chucky and other anime characters. People have protested dressed up as Pepe the Frog or holding the One Piece pirate flag, connecting Europe’s demonstrations to the symbols of global Gen Z protests, from Portland to Kathmandu.
Read more:
From anime to activism: How the ‘One Piece’ pirate flag became the global emblem of Gen Z resistance
Some students attending the October 17 protests told Le Monde “there’s no point in getting angry, so we might as well do it with a smile”. And that is precisely the point: both memes and spectacle can put joy, humour and playfulness at the centre, making grievances visible on the protesters’ own terms and generating viral images that compete with negative media coverage.
The fire in Limoges and the orchestra in Paris are not competing truths, and neither should cancel the other out. What these events have in common is the framing of protests as viral spectacles, staged for the cameras, digital platforms and distant audiences.
A burning building and a massive concert are easy to capture on camera, while struggles over housing, the cost of living and the deterioration of public services are not. Understanding protest therefore means looking beyond the image that travels furthest, fastest and most easily. It means asking who selected them, and whose account they serve when they go viral.

sources.headline: France’s ‘casseurs’: why the term fails to do justice to the extent of looting and spiralling unrest
sources.text:
Following widespread looting sprees and acts of violence occurring on the sidelines of the October 17 student protests, so-called “casseurs” seem to be the centre of attention. But the term, which comes from the French verb casser or “to break”, poses more questions than answers. The sociologist Paolo Stuppia examines the unprecedented situation many cities across France are having to contend with, and the complex combination of collective action whose motivations are unclear and the social media’s extreme agility.
The Conversation: How unprecedented are the scenes of looting that we witnessed on the sidelines of the October 17 demonstrations?
Paolo Stuppia: What may be unprecedented is the extent of the destruction of private property and the goods that have been stolen. It should be clear, however, that not all the looters can necessarily be sorted into identifiable groups, at least politically.
Indeed, as the politician Xavier Crettiez, the sociologist Isabelle Sommier and the historian François Audigier emphasised in 2021 in their joint project Violences politiques en France, the targets of acts of violence that are considered to be politically motivated can be determined both by technical constraints and the militant culture of the people involved. Let us recall Italy in the 1970s when autonomous activists spoke of “self-reduction” (the act of seizing goods or essential services), Maoists in France spoke of proletarian reappropriation. Their raid on Fauchon’s luxury grocery store on place de la madeleine and the redistribution of goods to slums and workers’ hostels that ensued went down in history as their biggest claim to fame.
Can we go as far as to say that the October 17 looting sprees were politically motivated? Even if we do not have all the details concerning the profiles of the people arrested, videos posted on social media and stolen goods being resold online tend to rule out the idea. That said, at least some of the targets were chosen haphazardly. While some are symbols of capitalism, like luxury stores, insurance companies, banks, multinationals, others included a number of more localised stores, small shops selling toys or video games; for example, which are rarely targets for such incidents.
If, especially since the alter-globalisation movement, we have seen the emergence of damage to property, primarily targeting symbols of capitalism and multinationals, in particular; this phenomenon goes hand in hand with “off the cuff” incidents by groups without any political affiliation, who join demonstrations to “get in on the act” in such a way that we are unable to determine whether it’s just a way of letting off steam or if it’s driven by a goal of redistributing goods – this weekend we witnessed some scenes of goods being redistributed, such as food being given to the homeless.
What do we know about casseurs’ profiles? When did they appear in the demonstrations and when did the term first appear in the media?
P.S.: Historically, the first research article on the casseur phenomenon can be traced back to the sociologist Gwenola Ricordeau. In France in the 1990s, as was the case during the student and high school movement of 1998, Ricordeau noticed that young people came to demonstrations to commit acts of vandalism or to mug people without having anything to do with the causes behind protest movements. They were driven by opportunism and also a desire to break up the monotony of everyday life.
The fact of disqualifying people by designating them as “criminals on the street” therefore ultimately leads us to riot-like phenomena, with or without the “looting” element, which are part of the continuity of “suburban revolt” or “city riots” which have gradually developed in working-class neighbourhoods since the second half of the 1970s. As we demonstrated alongside the sociologist Valérie Becquet in our book Géopolitique de la jeunesse, it forms a collection of pejorative and disqualifying terms pertaining to a so-called “dangerous youth”.
The term “casseur”, along with the derogatory term “racaille”, an old French term meaning rabble for example, widely resonated in the language of the media during the 2005 unrest to refer to a lumpenproletariat of young people who attacked both police and vandalised private property and a number of public services and property or street furniture, but whose actions were void of any political meaning.
October 17 mass protest movement: who are the casseurs? (France 24, October 2026, don’t forget to activate dubbing or subtitiles in English).
If we take the theory of labelling, we can understand that the term “casseurs” is linked to the stigma attached to young people from working-class neighbourhoods. But there can also be a second meaning: the phenomena in which France’s Mouvance autonome (a movement drawing its influences from anarchism and situationism that sets itself apart), is involved in scenes of outbreaks of violence and damage to property, even harm targeting individuals. However, we should first note that the movement has a history of claiming responsibility for its actions. The casseur stigma is also turned around and sometimes used with self-derision.
In 2006, during the protests over contrat première embauche or first job contract law, there were tensions between those who said “we aren’t” or “we don’t want casseurs”, others who said, “it’s the government and the employers – they are the casseurs”. And it was in this context that a banner that appeared in Rennes (in western France), ended up in Paris, claiming: “We are all casseurs.” As if to recognise the term for what it is: a historically vague label, covering different realities, and that the media has invited to every protest movement without fail over the past 30 years.
It’s a bit like the expression “black bloc”: “casseurs” is used to refer to people who resort to techniques that are out of order or who conjure up a considerable cause for concern among a certain part of public opinion, and yet the term remains very vague and is easily instrumentalised.
How is social media a gamechanger for law enforcement?
P.S.: There is a clear difference between fairly structured protest movements, even in an informal way, and the much more spontaneous use of social networks to stage action among young and very young people, such as filming themselves wearing football shirts as they leave Paris’ Place de la République.
We are facing a generation that is demonstrating a certain digital agility. There is a proliferation of platforms. In the days of the yellow vests, we were still largely using tools that came from the Internet of the 2000s, whether it was Instagram, Facebook, a bit of messaging, but not that much, and also Twitter. What we are now seeing is a new wave of social networks in action, with tools also designed to reduce control, like Snapchat, or Telegram, where content is extremely short-lived.
The question would then be: how do we adapt to these new ways of using social media? There is also the phenomenon of loops, which are difficult to infiltrate, with people who move very quickly and provide real-time support for those involved in the movements, on a rather confidential level. One of the hypotheses would be that, in this case, law enforcement is a bit helpless.
There is a quickfire of information, several levels of conversation, with public and private chatrooms, and more or less restricted groups. These real-time conversations are much more difficult to apprehend. Beyond messages that rapidly disappear on Snapchat, for example, a whole set of parameters specific to this universe must be taken into account: profiles feature scores related to the person’s activity; anyone who infiltrates is therefore almost immediately identifiable.
The combination of extremely agile social media and protesters’ mobility is very difficult to control. An example of this was the youth movements in Hong Kong in 2019-2020, which caused a lot of trouble for the authorities, even though it involved a police force with a tutelary government that could still be called authoritarian. Even they struggled to control the groups of young demonstrators operating via social networks, committing fragmented acts, with ten people in one place, ten at another, dispersing quickly. It makes you wonder how much of an information time lapse we are contending with . But that will be up to the parliamentary commission of inquiry to work out.
Interview by Aurélie Djavadi.

sources.headline: As French protests escalate into riots, they may prove a gift for Marine Le Pen’s right-wing party
sources.text:
Mass protests in France have spiralled into riots, with between 500,000 and 800,000 demonstrators in cities and towns across the country, most of them students. More than 100 police and many more protesters have been injured and up to 2,000 people have so far been arrested.
Major public buildings – such as the town hall in Limoges and the historic tourist office in Lyon – were destroyed, while other public buildings were damaged and hundreds of shops were looted by small groups of mainly young men.
The protests began in the working-class suburb of Créteil in southeastern Paris on September 21 when high school students demonstrated against poor conditions: dilapidated facilities, a shortage of teachers and inconvenient timetabling (schools in France often spread classes between 8am and 6pm, including Saturday mornings, leaving one clear afternoon).
This summer’s heatwaves were still being felt in September in classrooms with no cooling systems. Senior school students have been further frustrated by the inefficiencies and inequities of the Parcoursup university application online portal.
Many French schoolteachers share their students’ concerns with large classes and poor conditions – and salary scales which are comparatively low compared with other professions (police earn more, for example).
There are many other schools where facilities are poor and classes are large. Even so, no one expected the protests to spread so rapidly to another 700 schools across the country. There was widespread shock at the speed with which the protests spread, apparently without leaders or manifestos.
But the protests in comparatively wealthy parts of cities suggested there is more going on than just anger at cockroaches in the toilets.
1968 parallels
The parallels with May 1968 are important here. Then, it was predominantly university students who protested against a stultifying and traditional educational system. But they were also protesting against what they described as a société bloquée: a world of conservative politics and social hierarchies, and limited opportunities.
There is plainly a similar mood among high school students today that their life chances are limited by AI and the grim realities of climate change and international conflict.
Neither the centre-right government of Emmanuel Macron nor its likely right-wing successor, the Rassemblement National led by Marine Le Pen, appeals.
Similarly, the recent eruption of student and wider protests in Spain, Italy, Portugal and Belgium suggests the issues are not confined to the nature of secondary schooling in France alone.
In Spain, for example, the largest protests for many years have been primarily focused on access to affordable housing. Across the western world, the years since 2020 in particular have been marked by deep resentment from those whose lives were upended by pandemic restrictions, rising costs of living and housing crises. These combined have hit particular sections of society hard while others have benefited.
Now, this is being exacerbated by an energy crisis aggravated by war in the Middle East and Ukraine.
It is important to distinguish clearly between the protesting school students, their supporters and many teachers and parents, and the hooded, violent young people (mainly men) – popularly known as casseurs. These men smashed their way into shops, set fire to public buildings and attacked police.
Over recent decades, labour protests and those of the “yellow vests” (gilets jaunes, largely focused on cost of living issues) have also been the occasion for violent confrontation and property destruction on the margins. Such deliberately anti-social action represents a violent repudiation of the structures of French institutions and society. It has no claim to the legitimacy of a centuries-long tradition of collective protest in France.
Where will it end?
It is impossible to know just where the protests might lead. As in 1968, hostility over disruptions and property damage may cause a backlash against the students where there has until now been sympathy. It’s also possible divisions may again emerge between students and the union movement. Perhaps the protests will continue to spread through Europe.
Certainly, they have become a key factor in the looming French presidential elections of April 2027. French politics are broadly divided into three blocs that refuse to cooperate with each other: an extreme right, a centre-right and an extreme left.
It has been simple for Le Pen and other right-wing politicians to both promise she would reimpose discipline in schools, increase funding for police and target the casseurs as “obviously” illegal migrants to be deported.
The violence on the margins of what were massive, peaceful demonstrations has been an early Christmas present for her. It is also potentially ruinous for Jean-Luc Mélenchon and his left-wing La France Insoumise party, which has strongly backed the protests.
The immediate issue is whether Macron’s beleaguered government is able to respond to legitimate student demands in a way which might defuse the tensions within a deeply angry society.

sources.headline: French borrowing costs overtake US amid budget turmoil
sources.text: French borrowing costs continued to rise on Thursday, as investors fret that France’s government is struggling to pass a federal budget after public protests gripped the country.France’s bond market was hit with another bout of selling, with the difference between French and German 10-year borrowing costs – a metric for the risk premium attached to French debt – rising to its highest level in almost 15 years.The yield on the French 10-year bond – known as obligation assimilables du Trésor (Oat) – rose by nine basis points to 5.089% in early trading on Thursday, its highest level since July 2022. It broke across the 5% threshold on Wednesday for the first time since 2002.The move lifted France’s 10-year borrowing costs over the equivalent for US Treasury bonds for the first time since 2013.The volatility comes as the French government struggles to pass a budget for next year, while the country recovers from widespread protests that turned violent last weekend.A graph on how French and German 10-year bond yields have divergedTens of thousands of people had attended peaceful marches to demand more teachers and repairs to decrepit schools, but different groups clashed with police in cities including Paris, Bordeaux, Nice and Marseille in recent days.Public buildings were attacked, and thousands of shops and businesses were looted. The interior ministry said there had been nearly 2,400 arrests.Meanwhile, a parliamentary gridlock has blocked plans by the president, Emmanuel Macron, to increase the state pension age from 62 to 64 and a series of measures designed to rein in state spending.France’s budget deficit was 5.1% of gross domestic product in 2025, while its debt pile stood at 115.6% of GDP.It comes as the country also grapples with higher inflation triggered by the war in Iran, with many governments with big debt piles coming under acute pressure.Jim Reid, a market strategist at Deutsche Bank, said the sell-off in French government bonds was starting to ripple out to other countries, too.skip past newsletter promotionafter newsletter promotion“Among others, the Italian 10-year spread over [German bonds] widened 3.8 basis points to 116 basis points, while Spain’s widened 3.1 basis points to 66 basis points, marking its widest level since June 2025,” he said.Carsten Brzeski of the bank ING said rising yields had reinforced the European Central Bank’s “restrictive” monetary policy stance before its interest rate decision next week. The bank last raised its key interest rate to 2.5% in September.“The ECB is very likely to stay on hold next week and will delay any next rate hike decision to December,” he said.“Any solution to the current French fiscal woes could bring some relief to bond markets and allow the ECB to continue hiking rates. Without any solution, bond markets have taken over the ECB’s role, making rate hikes less likely.”

sources.headline: France hit by debt sell-off as violent protests unnerve investors
sources.text: France has been hit by a fresh wave of selling in its bond and stock markets after violent protests over the weekend led to thousands of arrests and left public buildings burned and hundreds of shops looted across the country.France protests escalate with riots, looting and 2,400 arrests - The LatestThe chaos has spooked investors as analysts worried that it would undermine Paris’s efforts to cut spending and reduce its debt.The yield on the government’s 10-year bonds rose by as much as 16 basis points to 4.94% on Monday. Yields rise when prices fall, and the bond market sell-off pushed France’s borrowing costs close to a 24-year high.This widened the difference between the French and German 10-year borrowing costs – which is a metric for the risk premium attached to French debt – towards its highest level in 14 years.Analysts at Goldman Sachs said European sovereign risk was back in focus, with fiscal concerns about France raising the question of whether there could be a repeat of the eurozone debt crisis of 15 years ago.“The risks of disorderly market escalation and real economy contagion look notably lower. But the fundamental fiscal challenges for some countries – especially in France – look harder now than in 2011-15,” the investment bank said.“The issue of how to deal with fundamental sovereign risk remains unresolved in the euro area, requiring credible fiscal consolidation.”The two-year French bond yield rose by nine basis points to 3.64%.Concerns about France’s instability knocked the euro down to a 17-month low against the pound on Monday morning, when sterling rose to €1.188.‘It’s hell’: residents reel after violent weekend riots across France – videoViolence erupted across France after weeks of relatively peaceful demonstrations over conditions in schools and the cost of living, prompting the French president, Emmanuel Macron, to condemn the “unbridled violence” in a televised address on Sunday night.Tens of thousands of people have attended peaceful marches to demand more teachers and repairs to decrepit schools, but different groups have clashed with police in cities including Paris, Bordeaux, Nice and Marseille.Jim Reid of Deutsche Bank said the protests “won’t make it easy for the international community to be totally comfortable buying OATs”, referring to French government bonds.“With France already facing a difficult fiscal backdrop and the 2027 election approaching, the weekend adds another layer of political risk for markets,” he said.The 30-year bond, which is a benchmark for the French government’s long-term cost of borrowing, rose by ten basis points to 5.46%.The rises will put further strain on France’s public finances as the government tries to pass a budget for next year to rein in its deficit.skip past newsletter promotionafter newsletter promotionFrance’s debt-to-GDP stood at 115.6% in 2025, while its budget deficit was 5.1%, compared with 94.3% and 4.3% respectively for the UK.The unrest adds to “concerns about the political and fiscal troubles in France”, said Neil Wilson, Saxo UK’s investor strategist.“It underscores how hard it will be for a government to enact the kind of spending restraint required to get the deficit down.”The French government is preparing a budget that would involve cutting pensions spending and funding for government departments, excluding defence. There are growing fears, however, that political pressure could derail the plans, which could push up borrowing further and add more to the country’s debt pile.The euro also slipped against the US dollar, down by 0.4% at one stage on Monday to $1.1197.France’s Cac 40 index, which tracks the biggest companies listed in Paris, fell by 1.4% , compared with a 1.1% drop on the pan-European Stoxx 600 index.French bank stocks were among the fallers, with Société Générale and BNP Paribas down more than 3%.Other European stock markets also weakened, with Italy’s FTSE Mib down 1.6% and Spain’s Ibex dropping by 1.9%.Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said investors were concerned that higher borrowing costs would increase France’s debt-servicing expenses, reducing its fiscal flexibility at a time when growth is already subdued.“But France is not alone,” he said. “Spain faces its own political constraints around budgets and fiscal reforms, although stronger economic growth provides some protection, while Italy’s substantial debt stock leaves it particularly sensitive to prolonged periods of elevated yields.”

sources.headline: Paris extends curfew as Marseille and Lyon ban protests after riots
sources.text: Paris is extending a partial curfew restricting movement in parts of the city until Monday, as Marseille and Lyon impose a total ban on protests this weekend. The Louvre, Orsay and Picasso museums in the French capital will also be closed on Saturday as more demonstrations are expected.France is still reeling from major disorder at the weekend, when large protests against the high cost of living and school conditions were overshadowed by riots and looting that saw business and historic buildings destroyed. In other parts of the country where protests have not been banned completely, only authorised union demonstrations will be allowed on Saturday, President Emmanuel Macron said. Interior Minister Jean-Didier Berger said police deployments would be increased by 20% compared to last weekend, after the government was accused of being blindsided by the scale of the unrest.France's justice minister said on Thursday that 217 people had been jailed over last weekend's disorder after being convicted in fast-track trials, with that number expected to rise.Gérald Darmanin said 2,700 people had been arrested across France and more than 1,000 have appeared in court.Half of those detained had no prior criminal record, he said, according to Le Figaro newspaper. Police in Paris said its curfew in Place de la République, where protesters gathered last weekend, and the Les Halles shopping area will be extended until Monday.Movement will be prohibited in both areas from 23:00 local time (21:00 GMT) until 06:00 the following morning, the prefecture for the capital city said, adding that it had been ordered by Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu.Public transport Marseille will be suspended on Saturday to try to prevent a repeat of the riots in the city.The city saw some of the worst violence last weekend and damage to more than 500 businesses. The prefecture for the Rhône region - which covers Marseille - said a curfew for minors would be extended to the entire population overnight on Saturday 24 October, from 23:00 until 05:00 (21:00 - 03:00 GMT). Similar announcements have been made in Nice in the south, Toulon on the south coast, the centre of Rouen in the north-west, and Grenoble in the east.Macron met intelligence services and ministers on Thursday, to prepare for the next national day of protests on Saturday."The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations. Those who want to continue to demonstrate, when they are trade union organisations, will have alternative routes proposed by the prefects," the French president announced. "When they're not union organisations, wherever possible, they'll be banned."He attacked what he called "political and even seditious acts organised by far-left groups that aim to bring down the Republic". Curfews were imposed in several cities in the aftermath of the weekend rioting, and Macron said the government wanted a return to calm.The gilets jaunes (yellow-vest) movement was behind many of last weekend's protests and Paris authorities have said several of their proposed marches have been banned.Partial curfews variously restricting the movement of young people and gatherings have been in place this week in cities including Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south as well as Lille and other towns in the north.Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu promised a "massive" deployment of police officers this week to deal with any unrest this weekend, but some officers have told French media they are not trained to deal with large crowds.Around 550,000 people took part in demonstrations on 17 October to protest rising fuel prices and the cost of living, which have escalated after weeks of student protests. Marches were largely peaceful and took place in several major French cities, including Paris, backed by unions, gilets jaunes and student groups. But they were marred by scenes of violence, looting and destruction.Lyon's tourism office was set on fire by demonstrators during last weekend's protests. In the city of Limoges, the clock tower and parts of the roof of the ornate city hall were engulfed in flames before collapsing on Saturday.A second suspect aged 66 was arrested on Thursday, after a man in his 30s was detained on suspicion of the attempted murder of police officers who were in the city hall when the fire started. The iconic Place de la République was vandalised in the capital, Paris, when groups of rioters took over parts of the city, wreaking havoc. The unrest has come as Macron enters the final months of his presidency, with elections scheduled for 18 April and 1 May next year.

sources.headline: Are the French police the most violent in the EU?
sources.text:
Videos of alleged police violence are going viral on French social media as a wave of protests grips France. One video shows the police beating a man to the floor then dragging him away unconscious. Another shows an officer grabbing a young man from behind, seemingly unprovoked, and dragging him by the neck. Another shows a young woman being hauled off with a twisted arm, screaming in pain. These videos could not be independently verified.
The French police have drawn renewed criticism from rights groups, not only because of their methods but also because of their use of stun grenades and rubber bullets. France has one of the most heavily armed police forces in Europe. During the student protests of the past weeks, several teenagers sustained life-changing injuries as a result: One had a hand blown off, one was blinded in one eye, another had his jaw broken.
France's protests grow
More than half a million people took to the streets in France on Saturday, most of whom protested peacefully, criticizing public sector cuts, the cost-of-living crisis and supporting students' demands for better conditions in classrooms.
Rioters took advantage, burning buildings, looting stores and lobbing projectiles at the police, creating a difficult situation for the officers and other emergency services.
The protests over the weekend followed a series of protests by high-school students, who barricaded school buildings to denounce a shortage of teachers and demand repairs to crumbling infrastructure.
More protests will be happening this weekend, with the French government saying it will even deploy military forces.
Some tools used by the French police are banned or rarely used in other countries Image: Manon Cruz/REUTERS
Weapons made for war?
The French police have a bigger arsenal than most European countries. For instance, officers use the so-called LBD-40, a type of gun used to fire rubber bullets.
Many countries, like the UK and Germany, mostly do not allow the use of rubber bullets in protests. In some European countries, like Spain, they are sometimes used but cause fewer injuries than in France.
"It is not a French specificity. But there are guidelines. There must be a certain distance," Anastassia Tsoukala, an associate professor of criminology at the University of Paris-Sud, told DW. "Even if you try to respect the guidelines, people may move and then all of a sudden they may lose one eye. So it's extremely dangerous."
Police in France routinely use tear gas, as do police in many other countries in Europe. In warfare, its use is actually forbidden under agreements like the Chemical Weapons Convention.
What makes the French police stand out from other forces is its use of stun grenades.
"These grenades contain a high level of explosive substances. So from this point of view, France is unique," said Tsoukala.
Minister of the Interior Laurent Nunez insists that weapons used by the police are "non-lethal." However, some of the equipment used by the force is classified by France's own internal security code as "war material."
France: Why students are taking to the streetsTo view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
French police: the 'most brutal' in the EU?
The police's use of these weapons has received renewed criticism after it resulted in injuries during the protests. The teenager who lost use of an eye is suspected of being hit at close range with a rubber bullet from an LBD-40.
"When we look at crowd control, it is clear that if we measure police brutality by the number of deaths amongst demonstrators or members of the crowd, and if we also measure it by the number of cases of maiming, the French police are the most brutal in the whole of the European Union," says Roche.
He points to the political context to understand the French police's equipment and how it is used today.
"The political authorities are free to decide on the police's equipment," the police expert says. "When LBDs were introduced into the [French] police force, they were intended for units like anti-organized crime units. This is the same weapon that is today used for crowd control. It gives an idea of how the way in which politicians in France think we can or should deal with political protest has evolved."Confrontation vs. de-escalation
Another difference between the French police and forces elsewhere is the methods. German police, for example, are supposed to try to avoid escalation.
Roche compares how protestors were moved in Lützerath, Germany, in 2023 to the more aggressive methods in Sainte-Soline, France, in 2023. Both places saw environmental protests.
"In Lützerath, dogs were used, there were some injuries but far fewer seriously injured people on both sides. In Sainte-Soline, the military police was sent in and used LBDs and grenades intensively. There were serious injuries amongst both police officers and demonstrators. Two protestors were left in a coma."
Police arrested protesters in the German town of Lützerath, but with less force than at similar protests in FranceImage: Federico Gambarini/dpa/picture alliance
When can police officers use force?
According to international standards set by the United Nations, use of force by officers of the law "should be exceptional," in the case of "prevention of crime" or "lawful arrest." Any use of force should follow a principle of "proportionality," which means no more than necessary to achieve its objective.
French Interior Minister Nunez has insisted in radio interviews that officers have largely respected this principle, which is also enshrined in French law, during the current protests.
However, rights group Amnesty International describes the police response to the current protests as "disproportionate" and calls upon French authorities to "act upon their human rights obligations."
The French branch of the League of Human Rights condemns the "violent repression" of the high school protest movement.
DW contacted two police unions and the French Interior Ministry for comment, but none responded before time of publication.
"It was very complicated to contain all the different groups," Interior Minister Nunez said in Marseille on Tuesday. "The police did a great job and there were a great number of crimes that were prevented thanks to their commitment."
Experts are critical of the police's actions.
"Public order is subordinated to human life and safety," Tsoukala said. "As a jurist I should say that this is a non-negotiable value."
Less oversight than in the UK and Denmark
The French police have no independent watchdog, only an internal division called the IGPN (General Inspectorate of the National Police) that can investigate when problems occur. The IGPN says it has opened at least 40 cases since the beginning of the latest protests.
Countries like the UK and Denmark investigate incidents differently, with independent watchdogs. However, Tsoukala criticizes leniency and a lack of transparency across Europe when incidents with the police occur.
"They are acquitted or they receive extremely light penalties," she said. "And I'm afraid this is the standard method to deal with police brutality cases across Europe."
Edited by: Carla Bleiker
