sources.headline: How a US political venture capital firm is trying to influence Brazil’s election
sources.text:
In the first round of Brazil’s elections on Oct. 4, 2026, Flávio Bolsonaro, of the right wing Liberal Party (PL), came in first with 47.03% of the valid votes, compared to 45.16% for the current leftist president and Workers’ Party (PT) candidate, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
The margin was just over 2.2 million votes, and the first polls for the runoff on Oct. 25 indicate a virtual tie. In a race like this, factors that would be marginal in a lopsided election become decisive. One of them comes from Washington and was little known in Brazil until September 2026, on the eve of the first round: Rockbridge Network.
A political venture capital firm
Rockbridge was founded in 2019 by the current US vice president, J.D. Vance — then a Silicon Valley investor — and Chris Buskirk, editor of the pro-Trump website American Greatness. In a 2021 brochure distributed to donors and circulated by the New York Times the following year, the network described itself as “a kind of political venture capital firm.” The idea was to bring together donors dissatisfied with the traditional Republican Party and invest their money in a portfolio of projects: its own media outlets, training personnel for a future U.S. administration, and voter mobilization in U.S. states.
The formula worked. In 2024, according to the Reuters news agency, the network had a budget of about US$75 million for the election cycle, focused on right-wing journalism, polling and voter mobilization in states critical to the US presidential election. A significant portion of its structure consists of entities that are not required to disclose their donors. Among the reported funders are Peter Thiel, co-founder and chairman of the technology company Palantir and Rebekah Mercer, one of the owners of the far-right American news site Breitbart.
Donald Trump participated by phone in a meeting of the network in April 2024, and months later chose Vance as his running mate. Since the Republican victory in the 2024 election, Rockbridge has served as a bridge between donors and the government: senior administration officials have begun giving presentations to its members.
Brazil is not the first foreign destination for Rockbridge’s activities. In September 2025, the network launched a branch in South Korea, chaired by Kim Hae-young, a former lawmaker from the center-left Democratic Party of Korea. The board includes former Prime Minister Kim Boo-kyum, of the same party; former Finance Minister Bahk Jae-wan, from a conservative administration; and Chung Yong-jin, chairman of the Shinsegae Group. In Seoul, Rockbridge positioned itself as a channel for elites on both sides of the political spectrum to gain access to the Trump administration. In Brazil, the approach would be different.
What Is Known About Rockbridge in Brazil
On Sept. 25, 2026, the Brazilian newspaper Folha de S.Paulo revealed that Rockbridge had begun setting up operations in the country. Documents obtained by Intercept Brasil detail the project. A business plan from April 2026, marked as “not for public release” and signed with the “Rockbridge Network Brasil” logo, described the operation as a “political venture capital fund” — an echo of the US parent company’s self-definition. Members’ annual dues would finance projects on three fronts considered “out of balance”: the press, universities, and the legislature.
A second document, confidential and unsigned, was addressed to Flávio Bolsonaro - son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, now jailed for attempting a coup after losing the 2022 presidential election. It proposed a Technology Council of 23 business leaders, 19 of whom were foreign, to directly advise the Liberal Party’s presidential candidate and bring American investors closer to a potential administration of his in sectors such as defense, energy, data centers, and rare earth metals. The text presented the council as useful “as a campaign tool” and “as a platform for government,” and hinted at investment commitments even before the inauguration. There is no evidence that the material reached the candidate, and several of the listed companies deny having been consulted.
The individuals involved, however, are close to Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign. Businessman Pedro Sang, identified in the document as the executive director of the Brazilian operation, told The Intercept that the council “was just an idea that never took off or moved forward.” Sang was introduced to Rockbridge through André Marinho, of the right wing Novo party, a candidate for governor of Rio and son of businessman Paulo Marinho, Flávio’s alternate in the Senate.
Marinho wrote a memo about a Brazil-US partnership on rare earths under a potential Flávio administration, which he now describes as a “hypothetical exercise.” Nine days after the file was created, Flávio said at CPAC, in Dallas, that Brazil was the solution for the United States to break free from its dependence on China for critical minerals.
In the new episode of the series Revelando, “Pátria submissa,” Wagner Moura discusses the ongoing agreement to hand over Brazil’s rare earth minerals to the US in the event of a Flávio Bolsonaro victory.
Tallis Gomes, founder of Easy Taxi, stated in April, on the Os Sócios podcast, that he was part of Rockbridge and that Flávio had asked him for written proposals for his government plan. Afterwards he told The Intercept that he is merely part of a networking group. On Oct. 1, allies of the Liberal Party’s candidate told Folha that businesspeople linked to the network produced reports and provided consulting services to the campaign.
Rockbridge denied for weeks that it had plans for Brazil, until it admitted that it had opened a company in the United States, Rockbridge Brazil LLC, registered in Wyoming in May. It claims that the initiative did not move forward, that the company never received funds or operated, and that Brazilians produced documents bearing its name without its consent. Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign denies having received foreign funds.
The legal dispute and the limits of evidence
The accusation of foreign campaign financing came from Renan Santos, then a presidential candidate for the Missão party, who claimed, without presenting evidence, that Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign was receiving money from the network indirectly. Based on this, Workers’ Party Congressman Lindbergh Farias filed a petition with the STF on Sept. 11. The Workers’ Party asked Justice Flávio Dino to order a Federal Police investigation, and Lula’s campaign took the case to Brazil’s Electoral Supreme Court (TSE), requesting records of meetings, contracts and expenses.
Brazilian election law prohibits donations from foreign entities to campaigns. So far, however, there is no public evidence that money from Rockbridge reached Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign, and it is unlikely that the courts will conclude any investigation before Oct. 25, the date of the presidential election’s runoff.
How to influence the election without making a donation
The debate focused on money, however, asks the wrong question. Rockbridge does not need to have transferred a single dollar to have influence in this election. It can do so through a number of other means.
The first is programmatic. The network offers Flávio Bolsonaro something no other candidate has: a direct channel to the inner circle surrounding the US vice president, who leads most polls for the likely Republican nomination in the 2028 U.S. presidential election. Rockbridge Brazil LLC was registered by Chris Applegate, who is in charge of Vance’s relationship with donors.
With part of Brazil’s exports subject to tariffs of up to 37.5% since July — as part of the second round of trade sanctions following the U.S. Supreme Court’s overturning of the 2025 tariff hike — the promise to repair relations with Washington holds electoral value, especially among business leaders and exporters.
The proposal for cooperation on rare earths — a resource in which Brazil holds the world’s second-largest reserves, second only to China — gives concrete substance to this promise. And it aligns with the priority of Trump’s economic diplomacy in the competition with China over supply chains. The candidate can present himself not only as Trump’s ideological ally but also as his preferred interlocutor.
The second is organizational. What Rockbridge sells in the United States is a method. Its 2021 brochure outlined plans for its own media outlets, influencer programs, and a “shadow government” to train staff, and the network funded voter mobilization in key states in 2024.
The Brazilian plan replicated this model. Even though the organization never formally operated in the country, knowledge circulates among people, and some of them, according to Flávio Bolsonaro’s own allies, have already worked on his campaign. In a runoff decided by just a few points, the ability to mobilize business leaders, fund campaign content, and get voters to the polls through legal and domestic channels may be worth more than any international transfer.
The third factor is the boomerang effect. Rockbridge could also prove decisive against Flávio Bolsonaro. Lula’s campaign has already incorporated this issue into its messaging, accusing Trump of wanting to “colonize” Brazil. In 2025, the US tariff hike boosted the president’s popularity by turning a trade dispute into a matter of sovereignty. The presence of a network linked to the US vice president surrounding a candidate offers the government the same narrative. The asset that brings Flávio Bolsonaro closer to business leaders is the same one that exposes him to nationalist voters.
What lies ahead after Oct. 25
Whatever the election results may be, this episode reveals a shift in how the American right projects its influence in Brazil. The Atlas Network, for example, supported a network of liberal think tanks in the country that promoted the neoliberal agenda and whose leaders rose to high-ranking positions in the Bolsonaro administration.
Rockbridge, for its part, exports something else: a model of organized political capital that links donors, candidates and access to the US government, with a specific economic agenda focused on critical minerals and technology, aligned with the rivalry with China. And the plan for Brazil does not end with the election: it calls for permanent councils for the press, universities, and the legislature, funded by members’ annual dues.
A comparison with South Korea highlights what is unique about the Brazilian case. In Seoul, the network brought together elites from both sides of the political spectrum around an alliance with Washington. In Brazil, it backed a single candidate. This is a form of private, partisan economic diplomacy that operates outside official channels and benefits one side of the political contest.
In 2019, Chris Buskirk spoke at Brazil’s Foreign Relations Ministry about how globalism would threaten national sovereignty. Seven years later, the network he heads listed 19 foreign executives to directly advise a presidential candidate.
The election law prohibits campaigns from receiving cash donations or donations valued in cash from foreign entities. Reports and consulting services, if proven, may fall under this category. But the promise of access to Washington and future investments has no declarable price, and that is precisely what Rockbridge offers. In a country split down the middle, this loophole could decide the next administration.

sources.headline: Brazil’s Sovereignty Is on the Ballot
sources.text:
At the time of writing, prediction markets favor Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro to win Brazil’s Oct. 25 presidential runoff. But only a few months ago, his candidacy appeared to be coming off the rails. In mid-May, the far-right senator became embroiled in a major corruption scandal following the publication of leaked messages that showed he had asked for roughly $27 million from a now-jailed former banker at the center of the biggest banking fraud in Brazilian history.
The funds—around $12 million of which were transferred to a Texas account linked to the candidate’s brother Eduardo—were purportedly to help finance a hagiographic biopic about their father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, who remains under house arrest for plotting a coup to overturn Brazil’s 2022 election. Soon after the scandal broke, Flávio’s poll numbers began to plummet. He urgently needed to change the subject.
The following week, U.S. President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio came to the rescue. On May 26, Trump received Flávio in the Oval Office for an unannounced photo-op. He told reporters that he had asked Trump to label Brazil’s biggest gangs as foreign terrorist organizations (FTOs). Rubio granted the designation two days later. Flávio was able to project political strength and shift the conversation from corruption to insecurity; his candidacy was once again secure.
The FTO classifications are yet another example of the Trump administration interfering in Brazilian politics, coming on top of politically motivated tariffs on Brazilian exports (which Eduardo lobbied for) and sanctions on the Supreme Court justice who prosecuted Jair Bolsonaro. They are not dissimilar to the administration’s aggressive efforts to influence recent elections in Argentina, Colombia, and Honduras.
Beyond their symbolic impact in an election year, it’s worth considering what the U.S. FTO designations could mean for Brazil’s sovereignty and strategic autonomy—especially if Flávio wins on Sunday. Brazilians have reason to fear that their country could become engulfed in Trump’s expanding war on what he calls “narco-terrorism.”
Waging war on regional drug trafficking organizations was a prominent campaign theme for Trump. In January 2023, he announced that he would “take down the cartels just as we took down ISIS,” ostensibly to combat the fentanyl epidemic in the United States.
Within weeks of his 2025 inauguration, the president began to make good on his promises, designating several Latin American criminal organizations as FTOs—including the Sinaloa and Jalisco New Generation cartels and gangs such as MS-13 and Tren de Aragua. It was the first time that any U.S. administration had applied this classification to drug-trafficking organizations with no apparent political agenda.
In August of that year, Rubio declared that cartels are “armed terrorist organizations, not simply drug dealing organizations,” placing them in the same national-security framework as al-Qaeda, Boko Haram, and the Islamic State.
Starting in September 2025, this doctrinal shift servedas justification for a series of unprecedented—and seemingly unlimited—lethal military actions in the Caribbean, Central America, and eastern Pacific. In a campaign later dubbed “Operation Southern Spear,” U.S. military vessels have struck dozens of boats allegedly controlled by drug-trafficking FTOs, killing their occupants (239 people, at last count) without arrest or trial and without presenting evidence that they were carrying drugs. The identities of most of those killed remain unknown—even to the U.S. military.
The strikes have done nothing to address the fentanyl trade, since the deadly drug overwhelmingly comes to the United States by land, from Mexico. Nor have they significantly disrupted the cocaine trade, with recent reports—including an assessment by the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration—indicating that traffickers have adapted their routes.
But the policy has achieved something else: FTO designations transformed a law enforcement issue into a military one, paving the way for an expansion of U.S. military activity across the Western Hemisphere.
The most dramatic expression of this shift so far was the Jan. 3 U.S. military attack on Venezuela and abduction of the President Nicolás Maduro to face drug trafficking charges in the United States. The attack was the first of its kind in South America and killed an estimated 75 people. The State Department linked it to a recent FTO designation, despite providing no real evidence that Venezuela’s government played a leadership role in the hemispheric drug trade.
The unauthorized U.S. military campaign across the Americas has generated concern in the U.S. Congress, which has the sole authority to send the military into hostilities. It should also concern Brazil. The designation of Brazilian criminal organizations as FTOs transforms them, at Washington’s discretion, from targets of Brazilian law enforcement into potential targets of U.S. military force.
Under incumbent left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Brazil would most certainly continue to resist the pressure of such a designation on the country’s jurisdiction and sovereignty. But under Flávio, U.S. military operations on Brazilian soil are a real possibility. In response to an October 2025 social media post from U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth about a lethal strike on a boat in the eastern Pacific, the far-right candidate said “how envious” he was and invited Hegseth “to spend a few months here helping us fight these terrorist organizations.”
Allowing for U.S. military intervention in Latin America is also one of the objectives of the Shield of the Americas, a new U.S.-driven alliance in which member governments—most of them right-wing allies of Trump—appear to be playing a subordinate role to Trump’s expanding regional military campaign.
In a September meeting of the alliance in New York, participating governments endorsed a sweeping declaration drafted by the Trump administration, reportedly with minimal input from other members. The declaration calls for invoking the 1947 Rio Treaty, a Cold War-era hemispheric security treaty that mirrors NATO’s Article 5 mutual defense clause. It would facilitate collective action against nonstate criminal organizations, potentially opening the door to foreign intervention in those countries.
The governments also committed to individual and collective action against the 24 criminal organizations that the U.S. State Department classified as FTOs, including the two Brazilian gangs. “If you can’t [deal with the criminal organizations], we’ll do it for you,” Trump said.
During his May 26 meeting with Trump, Flávio reportedly promised that, if elected, Brazil would join the Shield of the Americas. He later repeated the pledge on at least two occasions.
For Brazil, the stakes could hardly be higher. Unlike many of its Latin American neighbors, Brazil has long aspired to strategic autonomy, building industrial, military, and technological capabilities to defend its sovereignty without relying on a great-power patron. That ambition has produced an increasingly sophisticated defense industry. It has also shaped Brazil’s approach to the Amazon and the South Atlantic, where its armed forces have traditionally regarded control of territory, borders, and strategic resources as a national security issue.
Ecuador offers the most obvious and disturbing preview of what Washington’s war on narco-terrorism could mean for Brazil. Under President Daniel Noboa, the country has embraced an increasingly militarized security strategy, underwritten by deeper U.S. support, largely without stemming the ever-growing violence in the country. Ecuadorian forces have been implicated in allegations of enforced disappearances, extrajudicial killings, torture, and arbitrary detention. Human Rights Watch even documented torture during a U.S.-Ecuadorian joint operation that culminated in the bombing of a dairy farm.
At sea, U.S. forces have attacked, intercepted, and destroyed Ecuadorian fishing vessels. One boat, the Fiorella, disappeared along with eight crew members in January. The circumstantial evidence strongly suggests that U.S. forces were involved, although the U.S. military has denied it. The Washington Post subsequently reported that mysterious attacks on Ecuadorian vessels formed part of a covert CIA program. In August and September alone, U.S. forces intercepted and destroyed eight more Ecuadorian fishing vessels, detaining more than 140 crew members and drawing allegations of abuse. An Ecuadorian judge recently acquitted 32 of these crew members, stating that there was no evidence that they had committed illegal acts.
Meanwhile, Noboa is opening Ecuador ever further to U.S. military deployments. Last year, the State Department, at Noboa’s request, designated two Ecuadorian gangs as FTOs. In March, U.S. Southern Command and the Ecuadorian Army began carrying out joint military operations targeting these gangs, which they referred to as “narco-terrorists.”
Despite an Ecuadorian constitutional prohibition on foreign bases, U.S. Air Force personnel are stationed at Ecuador’s Manta base, with no scheduled departure, and U.S. military aircraft are operating from the Taura Air Base. In early September, the commander of the Ecuadorian Air Force made an official request for guidelines regarding the operational control of Taura and insisted that Ecuador should retain operational and administrative control. Noboa removed him from his post two days later.
Recent reports indicate that the Trump administration is now sending hundreds more U.S. troops to Latin America and has redirected tens of millions of dollars in military assistance intended for Europe and the Middle East to Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Panama. Trump has no interest in respecting other countries’ constitutional guarantees and sovereignty—not Ecuador’s, and most certainly not Brazil’s.
After Brazil’s first-round vote, Trump heralded Flávio’s two-point lead as a “close, but a very, very big victory.” It’s clear—whether through weaponized tariffs, sanctions, or FTO designations—that Trump, Rubio, and other administration officials have tried to shape the outcome of the Brazil’s presidential election. For them, acquiring Brazil as a pliant and politically indebted partner in the administration’s hemispheric campaign would be the ultimate prize, following recent far-right victories in Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, and Honduras.
Ultimately, Trump’s regional project—which he has unsubtly dubbed the “Donroe Doctrine”—extends beyond a hegemonic military agenda. It is, as his National Security Strategy announced in 2025, also about securing privileged access to hemispheric natural resources, especially critical minerals, while seeking to reduce and displace the region’s growing commerce with China. Flávio has presented Brazil as the answer to U.S. dependence on China for rare earths and promised Washington a strategic minerals partnership.
Lula has put forward a starkly different model. He has offered the Trump administration far-reaching police and financial cooperation against organized crime while rejecting Washington’s unilateral FTO designations as a threat to Brazilian sovereignty. Rather than embracing Trump’s plan for U.S. hemispheric dominance, he has continued to advocate for multilateralism and strategic autonomy, avoiding too much dependence on either the United States or China.
As Brazilians vote on Oct. 25, they should be aware that they will be making a strategic decision about whether their country’s security and resources should become integrated into a militarized, U.S.-led hemispheric architecture that—as the case of Ecuador clearly illustrates—leads to subordination while likely doing nothing to curb violence. Or whether they wish to remain subject to sovereign decisions made in Brasília.

sources.headline: The Banking Scandal Upending Brazil’s Election
sources.text:
Brazilians voted in the first round of the country’s presidential election on Oct. 4, sending Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro—the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro—and President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva to a runoff. Another key race was decided that day: In congressional elections, right-wing parties triumphed and are expected to hold at least 45 of 81 seats in the Senate.
Brazil’s Senate confirms (and can remove) justices on the Supreme Court, whose expanding judicial reach has made it a central arbiter of Brazilian democracy. Decisions by the bench could yet shape the outcome of the runoff, set for Oct. 25.
On Sept. 15, Chief Justice Edson Fachin convened a televised session to decide whether Justice Alexandre de Moraes—who oversaw Jair Bolsonaro’s prosecution and is reviled by the far right—should be investigated by the Federal Police. (Brazilian law requires courts to authorize investigations into their own members.) The justices never reached a decision: They split on a procedural motion, with Moraes voting on his own case, before Justice Flávio Dino asked for up to 90 days to study the file. That clock runs until mid-December—well after the runoff.
The case swirling around Moraes stems from the collapse last year of Banco Master, a midsize Brazilian lender. The scandal—like the Operation Car Wash investigation of the mid-2010s—has ensnared many members of Brazil’s political and business elite. Federal Police hope to examine whether Moraes improperly assisted Master’s controlling shareholder, Daniel Vorcaro, and whether that conduct was connected to a legal services contract between Master and Moraes’s wife’s law firm. Moraes denies wrongdoing. He has not been charged with a crime.
The scandal has become a hot topic on the campaign trail, and one likely to benefit Flávio. By putting off a decision on whether to investigate Moraes, the Supreme Court has handed Flávio a rallying cry, left Lula defending an institution that he has no plan to reform, and made the new right-wing Senate the arbiter of the court’s future.
Prior to its collapse, Banco Master held only 0.57 percent of Brazil’s banking assets. But its unique business model made it significant.
The bank sold certificates of deposit paying up to 140 percent of the interbank benchmark rate, far above what large banks offered. It leaned on the Credit Guarantee Fund, an insurer financed by member banks that covers up to about $49,000 per investor. (Although privately funded, the fund operates under government-set rules, and eligible banks are required to join and contribute.) This allowed Master to raise money without investors scrutinizing what it bought, including illiquid assets and credit portfolios that, according to investigators, lacked adequate backing.
Master also drew on public money. Banco de Brasília (BRB), a lender controlled by the government of the Federal District, bought Master’s credit portfolios. In March 2025, BRB agreed to buy 58 percent of the bank. The Central Bank blocked the deal that September and shut Master down on Nov. 18. The Credit Guarantee Fund repaid roughly $7.5 billion to about 800,000 savers, so taxpayers did not cover that bill. But BRB’s losses fall on the public: Federal Police found that BRB paid about $1.4 billion for Master portfolios before finishing at least one of its required risk assessments. BRB has since asked the district government for fresh capital.
Master’s reach went beyond finance: Vorcaro told police that he had friends in all branches of government, and the case has drawn in politicians across the political spectrum.
Ibaneis Rocha, the former Federal District governor, called the occasion of the proposed acquisition “a day of celebration,” and he left office in March to run for the Senate. He dropped out of the race in July, after the BRB president whom he had appointed was jailed.
Police say Master’s staff drafted an amendment to a proposed constitutional reform to quadruple the Credit Guarantee Fund’s per-depositor coverage that Sen. Ciro Nogueira, Jair Bolsonaro’s former chief of staff, introduced in Congress in 2024. Police have also said that Nogueira received monthly payments of up to roughly $98,000 from Vorcaro and figures associated with Master. Nogueira denies wrongdoing.
The Supreme Court took over the Master investigation because it involves members of Congress, who in Brazil can only be investigated with the Supreme Court’s authorization—and tried by the court itself. Justice Dias Toffoli was initially assigned to the case. He stepped aside in February after police flagged that funds managed by Vorcaro’s brother-in-law had a stake in a resort from a company partly owned by Toffoli and his brothers. Toffoli’s office has said he never had a friendship with Vorcaro.
The case was then reassigned to Justice André Mendonça, a Jair Bolsonaro appointee.
The scandal has reached both presidential campaigns, though not in the same way. Flávio’s exposure is direct: In May, Intercept Brasil published audio of him asking Vorcaro for money to finish Dark Horse, a biopic about his father. Flávio first denied any connection to Vorcaro, then acknowledged seeking the sponsorship, which he described as legitimate private investment.
Records from Brazil’s financial intelligence unit trace about $12.3 million from a Vorcaro-linked company to a Texas fund that managed the film’s money and is run by an ally of Flávio’s brother Eduardo, who successfully lobbied the Trump administration to sanction Moraes. Police documents do not link the money to Flávio’s personal accounts. In July, Mendonça authorized a formal investigation into possible corruption, money laundering, and currency evasion connected to the financing of Dark Horse. Neither brother has been charged in connection with the film’s financing.
Lula’s exposure is indirect. He is not implicated in wrongdoing, according to tax records reviewed by Reuters, though he met with Vorcaro in December 2024. This June, police executed search warrants targeting Sen. Jaques Wagner, who was then the Senate leader, on suspicion that he had advanced Master’s interests in exchange for benefits for relatives. Wagner, a member of Lula’s Workers’ Party, denies wrongdoing. He has since resigned from his leadership post.
For Lula, the larger liability is Moraes. Much of the Brazilian electorate places the justice and the president in the same camp—never mind that Moraes was appointed by right-wing former President Michel Temer.
Flávio has campaigned on the perceived link, saying, “Anyone voting for Lula is voting for Alexandre de Moraes.” Lula has responded by demanding an investigation of everyone implicated in the Master scandal, “no matter who it hurts.” Moraes is also a frequent target of tech entrepreneur Elon Musk, who called him an “evil dictator cosplaying as a judge” during a 2024 clash over court orders that led to X’s temporary suspension in Brazil.
Banco Master signed a three-year legal services agreement, potentially worth roughly $25.7 million, with a law firm where Moraes’s wife is partner. Federal Police investigators have said that metadata from a draft of the agreement shows a username linked to the justice, which they read as a sign that he edited the document. The firm says Moraes reviewed the contract only for potential conflicts of interest and that it never represented Master in court. Editorials in three major Brazilian newspapers have called on him to step down.
Master’s access extended deep into Brazil’s legal and law enforcement establishment. In April 2024, Master sponsored a forum in London and paid for the appearance of former British Prime Minister Tony Blair, who debated Vorcaro. Participants included Moraes, Justices Gilmar Mendes and Toffoli, Prosecutor General Paulo Gonet, and Federal Police Director-General Andrei Rodrigues. Messages on Vorcaro’s phone show him telling an associate that he needed to run the guest list by “Alexandre.”
The Federal Police report records Vorcaro’s claim, but it notes that investigators did not confirm with Moraes whether he had requested or approved the list. Should proceedings against Moraes move forward, every office that would have to investigate, charge, or judge him for potential wrongdoing was represented in that London room.
The court’s paralysis has become a campaign asset for Flávio. Every week without a ruling on Moraes lets Flávio attack the court further.
But it’s unclear whether the scandal has truly impacted the presidential race. In a survey conducted Sept. 8-10 by the polling firm Datafolha, 85 percent of respondents said the Moraes revelations had not changed their vote; 4 percent reported changing their choice, while another 7 percent said the revelations had left them uncertain. The same survey found that 76 percent think that Brazilian Supreme Court justices have too much power.
The Senate is where the court’s future will be settled. Jair Bolsonaro picked allied candidates to build a majority capable of impeaching justices, which requires two-thirds of the Senate, or 54 votes. Counts of incoming senators who back impeachment range from 48 to 54, depending on the survey. Flávio has promised to limit rulings by individual justices, end the court’s original criminal jurisdiction over members of Congress, and pursue amnesty for his father, alongside Moraes’s impeachment. Lula has proposed no structural change to the court.
Either way, the next president will likely appoint four of the court’s 11 justices. (Brazilian Supreme Court justices must retire by the age of 75.) One seat has been empty since April, when the Senate rejected Lula’s nominee, Jorge Messias—the first such rejection since 1894. Three more seats will open through mandatory retirements by December 2030.
The deeper problem will outlast the runoff. In 2024, I argued that Brazil’s democracy, for all its defects, was in no danger of falling apart, and I still believe that. But my view of the court has moved more in the past year than in the previous 10. Allegations against a justice are investigated under the court’s supervision, charged by the prosecutor general, and tried by colleagues. In this case, the prosecutor general appears in the evidence.
That loop has structural roots. In 2025, the court issued 116,170 decisions, and around 80 percent of them came from individual justices. The scholars Diego Werneck Arguelhes and Leandro Molhano Ribeiro call the pattern ministrocracia, or rule by individual justices. The court also writes its own conduct rules. In 2023, it struck down a statute barring judges from cases involving clients of their relatives’ law firms. The National Council of Justice, which disciplines the rest of the judiciary, has no jurisdiction over its members.
Complacency would leave that loop intact, but a court purged by a Senate eager for revenge is no guarantee of accountability. The Senate has never removed a justice, and the first impeachment would set a precedent that any future majority could invoke.
Most of the remedy lies in the court’s own hands. It could require justices to step aside from cases involving themselves or their relatives—which Moraes did not—send major rulings by a single justice to the full court; and assign cases at random, with no exceptions.
“Either we limit ourselves,” warned Fachin, the chief justice, in January, “or there may be limitation by an external power.”
Whoever wins Brazil’s presidency will inherit four Supreme Court seats to fill; a decision on Moraes due in December; and a public that, by roughly 4 to 1, thinks that the justices have too much power. The question for Brazil’s next government is not whether the Supreme Court will be constrained, but who will write those constraints.

sources.headline: Lula says rival should be disqualified over alleged Meta interference ahead of Brazil vote
sources.text: Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's campaign has requested the disqualification of right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro in the lead up to the final round of the presidential election on Sunday over alleged interference by social media company Meta.In a petition filed to the country's top electoral court on Wednesday, the leftist incumbent president accused Meta, the tech giant behind Whatsapp, Instagram and Facebook, of limiting its content to boost Bolsonaro's campaign.In response, Bolsonaro filed a petition seeking to disqualify Lula over what he said was the mass dissemination of government posts on WhatsApp.The company has denied the campaigns have been treated unequally.It comes after UN experts said on Wednesday that they were concerned about reports of discrepancies in the ability of each campaign to reach voters on Meta's platforms.A report led by the UN's special rapporteur on freedom of expression said Meta must ensure a level playing field online during the election.It cited incidents including "temporary interruptions of one candidate's campaign account; differences in audience engagement, user feeds, view counts and reach; restrictions on that campaign's Instagram posts". "Information, including from Meta employees, suggests that accounts linked to one side of the presidential race were disproportionately curtailed," it read. Meta has denied taking action to favour one side of the election and has said it would comply with an order from a Brazilian court to treat Bolsonaro and Lula equally. Lula's campaign had previously filed a complaint alleging that accounts and content related to Bolsonaro were boosted. Users also reported that Meta's artificial intelligence tools were not generating images related to Lula.Brazilians will head to the polls on Sunday as Lula seeks a fourth term in office.Bolsonaro beat Lula in the first round of voting on 4 October by a narrow margin, but fell short of the 50% of valid votes needed to win outright.On Wednesday, Lula's campaign filed a petition to Brazil's Superior Electoral Court (TSE) for Bolsonaro and Alfredo Gaspar, his candidate for vice-president, to be investigated over "abuse of economic power and improper use of social network". The petition also seeks to make Bolsonaro ineligible to stand for election for eight years following the 2026 election.Meanwhile, Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of convicted former president Jair Bolsonaro, accused his rival of "abuse of political and economic power". He claims the government has used personal data taken from official databases to send mass messages on Whatsapp to promote social programmes. Opinion polls suggest Sunday's run-off will be extremely close, with little separating the two as Brazil's 159 million registered voters prepare to go to the ballot boxes.
